sps.name: Texas connections
sps.track: Whether Texas resumes approving large data centre connections: statements and measures from the incoming Governor and Legislature that would extend, widen or lift the pause; the audit of the queue; and, behind those, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) queue of large loads of 75 megawatts or more and the capacity approved to energise.
sps.trigger: Positive if approvals grow faster than about 2 gigawatts a year, the approved share rises and the queue stops growing.
sps.headline: Paused
sps.summary: Approvals on hold since 3 Aug 2026; the Governor-elect has pledged a moratorium
sps.latest: The Governor-elect has pledged a moratorium on data centre approvals until the Legislature passes new protections; she takes office on 19 Jan 2027 and can replace the current directives. Approvals to energise large data centres have been paused since 3 Aug 2026, and passing the audit does not by itself restart them. She repeated the call on 19 Nov 2026 and accepted that she cannot stop sites already under construction. A Senate bill filed for the session that opens on 12 Jan 2027, reported as Senate Bill 338 with 17 senators behind it, all but one of them Republican, would from 1 Sep 2027 limit new data centres to water-saving cooling, require yearly reports of water use and refuse a grid connection to sites that fall short. It is a filed bill, not law, and it neither extends nor lifts the current pause. Since 12 Nov, environmental permit reviews have resumed. The queue stood at about 475 gigawatts in June 2026, of which about 9 (roughly 2%) had approval.
sps.next: Audit report 10 Dec 2026; Legislature convenes 12 Jan 2027; new Governor 19 Jan 2027
sps.sources: ERCOT large-load status updates and monthly operational overview; Public Utility Commission of Texas filings
sps.verify: The linked update confirms the pause and the audit date. Senate Bill 338 has now been read directly (https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/90R/billtext/pdf/SB00338I.pdf): it would take effect on 1 Sep 2027, allow only water-saving cooling, require yearly water-use reports and bar a grid connection for sites that do not comply; it contains no pause. The count of 17 senators is from a press report (KCBD, 19 Nov 2026). The queue of about 474 gigawatts and about 8.9 gigawatts approved to energise in June 2026 are confirmed in the grid operator's presentation to the Texas Senate of 29 Jul 2026 and its monthly overview for June. The Governor-elect's pledge and remarks, her powers and the resumed permit reviews come from a law-firm briefing and press reports, not from primary documents.

sps.latest: Is the queue growing? Yes. calls.bottom_line: Power stays Severe to 2030. It eases to Moderate after 2030 only if new turbines, the PJM backstop auction and Texas's new 765 kilovolt lines arrive on time, and Texas resumes connecting data centres. On-site power offers a partial way round the queue. Near-term data point the other way.

key.label: Eases to Minor if
key.text: Zero-water, closed-loop cooling becomes the norm for new capacity; states fund water supply ahead of data centre demand; hub utilities expand reclaimed water; growth tilts to water-rich basins.

calls.depends: Water stays a cost and a siting filter, not a hard stop, as developers adapt instead of leaving. Waterless cooling uses more electricity, and most of a data centre's water footprint sits in power generation that operators do not control. It intensifies to Severe if states turn disclosure rules into hard limits, drought leads utilities to refuse supply, or Colorado River cuts deepen.
calls.bottom_line: Water holds at Moderate in both periods: it adds cost and steers where sites go, but developers adapt with closed-loop cooling and reclaimed water instead of leaving. It intensifies to Severe if states write hard limits into law or drought leads utilities to refuse supply, and eases to Minor if waterless cooling becomes the norm.

sps.headline: Disclosure, not limits
sps.summary: State rules so far mostly require reporting. Texas Senate Bill 338 is proposed, not law; no Arizona statewide pause bill has been found
sps.latest: Rules are tightening, so far mostly through disclosure. From 1 Jan 2027 California requires a water-supply assessment before approving a data centre and makes developers fund the water infrastructure they need. Virginia, New Jersey and Utah now require water reporting. Locally, Marana will not supply drinking water to data centres, and Mesa, Avondale and Phoenix cap industrial water use. Proposed: Texas Senate Bill 338 (water-efficient cooling for new data centres), under a Governor-elect who has pledged to pause approvals. No Arizona statewide pause bill has been found yet.
sps.next: Texas Legislature convenes 12 Jan 2027; Arizona session opens Jan 2027
sps.sources: Texas Legislature Online; Arizona Legislature; state bill trackers

sps.name: Colorado River shortage
sps.track: Whether Lake Mead falls below 1,010 feet in the Bureau of Reclamation's monthly 24-Month Study projections, and how deep the next guidelines cut.
sps.trigger: Negative if Lake Mead is projected below 1,010 feet, which triggers consultation on deeper cuts, or if the next guidelines (from 2029) cut beyond 1.25 million acre-feet.
sps.headline: 1.25 million acre-feet cut a year
sps.summary: Lower Basin deliveries for 2027–28 are cut by that amount. The November study keeps Lake Mead above the 1,010-foot trigger, at a low of 1,014 feet
sps.latest: The Colorado River, which supplies the Phoenix, Tucson and Las Vegas hubs, reached record lows in August 2026. Lower Basin deliveries are cut by 1.25 million acre-feet a year in 2027 and 2028; if the Lower Basin states carry out their proposed sharing agreement, Arizona's share of the cut is 760,000 acre-feet, about 27% of its normal allocation. Under the 2027–28 operating guidelines, a most-probable projection of Lake Mead below 1,010 feet starts consultation on further action. The Bureau of Reclamation's November 2026 study, of 16 Nov, keeps the lake above that line: its most-probable runs reach a low of 1,014.0 feet in July 2027 (1,022.0 feet if 7 million acre-feet are released from Lake Powell), and only the minimum-probable run falls below 1,010 feet, from April 2028. The September and October studies are reported to have shown the lake below 1,010 feet in July 2027; both predate this call's baseline of 23 Nov 2026.
sps.next: December 24-Month Study, mid-December 2026; summer 2027 low point
sps.sources: US Bureau of Reclamation 24-Month Study; US Department of the Interior

history.note: Reclamation's November 24-Month Study read directly; owner kept the status at Not yet on 25 Nov 2026
history.brief: The November study keeps Lake Mead above the 1,010-foot trigger, at a most-probable low of 1,014 feet in July 2027

sps.verify: The November study (linked; also https://www.usbr.gov/lc/region/g4000/24mo_MIN.pdf), the 2027–28 operating guidelines and the Interior Department's release of 21 Aug 2026 were read directly. The earlier statement that the framework allows cuts of up to 3 million acre-feet with central Arizona first in line was not found in the documents read and has been removed.

sps.name: Spain's final rules
sps.track: Whether the data centre decree is approved before the general election, and its final terms.
sps.trigger: Watch the 80% hourly renewables match, the 10 megawatt threshold and the five-year phase-in.
sps.headline: In force
sps.summary: Spain's decree took effect on 22 Nov 2026 with the 80% hourly renewables match kept; a court challenge is announced and the election of 29 Nov lies ahead
sps.latest: Spain's royal decree on data centres (Royal Decree 1032/2026) was published in the official gazette on 21 Nov 2026 and has been in force since 22 Nov. The Council of Ministers approved it on 20 Nov, nine days before the general election. The terms this signpost watches are all in the published text. It applies to data centres with a grid access capacity of 10 megawatts or more, including projects that hold grid permits but are not yet connected; sites already connected are outside it. There are two separate 80% tests. In every hour, at least 80% of the electricity used must be backed by renewable power generated in that same hour. And 80% of total consumption must come from self-generation or long-term contracts with renewable or storage plants in Spain that are no more than 36 months older than the data centre, with exceptions that include solar plants which had no such contract when the decree took effect. For five years there is an easier route for sites able to cut their demand to zero when the grid operator calls: 60% in peak-tariff hours until the end of 2028, then 70% in peak hours and 60% in the next tariff band; it is open only to sites operating before 31 Dec 2030. Projects that hold permits have six months to show they comply or the permits lapse; pending applications are refused after three months; either can withdraw within six months without losing its deposits. A site that falls short pays a monthly charge of between €6 and €25 per megawatt-hour on the test for new renewable supply, and between €2 and €16 on the hourly test. The published text does not contain the loss of grid-access rights for up to three years that was reported at approval; it says permits can be suspended or revoked only as existing laws provide. What is not settled: the data centre industry association said on 23 Nov 2026 that it would go to the Supreme Court within days and ask for the decree to be suspended; no filing had been confirmed when this was written. The regional governments of Aragón and Madrid have said they will also challenge it. The main opposition party, the Partido Popular (People's Party), has repeated that it would repeal the decree, and the general election is on 29 Nov 2026. Why the opposition objects: its economy spokesman said the decree in practice prohibits new data centres and that the party would replace it with a law that allows them to be built. The regions it governs, among them Aragón and Madrid, host most of the large projects. The government's case: the energy minister said data centres have already been granted about 15 gigawatts of grid access, roughly 40% of Spain's peak demand, and that without the decree households and businesses would pay about €5 billion more on their bills and industry about 25% more for energy.
sps.next: General election 29 Nov 2026; any Supreme Court filing and ruling on suspension; deadlines for pending applications (about 22 Feb 2027) and permit-holders (about 22 May 2027)
sps.sources: Spain's official gazette; Council of Ministers references; energy ministry; Council of State

sps.latest: Spain's royal decree on data centres (Royal Decree 1032/2026) was published in the official gazette on 21 Nov 2026 and has been in force since 22 Nov. The water rule is in the published text: data centres must reach class A, the top class for water use on the European Union's data centre label, once that label exists. Until then the ceiling is a water-use ratio of 0.1 or less, calculated under the European Union's reporting rules; the decree gives the figure without a unit (the draft gave it as litres of water per kilowatt-hour). The text now shows who is covered and when. There is no separate water threshold: the rule applies to every data centre with a grid access capacity of 10 megawatts or more that is applying for grid access or holds permits but was not yet connected on 22 Nov 2026, which is wider than the draft's new sites. Sites already connected are not covered. The level must be met one year after a site starts operating. The text has no exemption for reclaimed or non-drinking water. Projects under European Union digital-sovereignty programmes, such as AI gigafactories, get easier steps: 0.4, then 0.2, then 0.1 for those starting from 2030. What is not settled: the data centre industry association said on 23 Nov 2026 that it would go to the Supreme Court within days and ask for the decree to be suspended; no filing had been confirmed when this was written. The regional governments of Aragón and Madrid have said they will also challenge it. The main opposition party, the Partido Popular (People's Party), has repeated that it would repeal the decree, and the general election is on 29 Nov 2026. The opposition's objections are aimed at the electricity rules; none found so far is aimed at the water rule, but a repeal or suspension would remove both. The government's case is that data centres' demand on the grid would otherwise raise bills for households and industry.

sps.headline: 12-month cap proposed
sps.summary: The proposed Cloud and AI Development Act would cap permitting in acceleration zones at 12 months; unlikely to bite before about 2029
sps.latest: The European Union's proposed Cloud and AI Development Act would require each member state to designate at least one data centre acceleration zone and would cap permitting there at 12 months from a complete application. In the Council, the Irish Presidency's first compromise text on the data centre part was on the agenda of a working party on 24 Nov 2026; no account of the discussion has been found. A Presidency progress report of 13 Nov says the compromise gives member states 12 months, not 6, to designate a zone and moves the date the act applies from 12 to 18 months after it enters into force. A progress report goes to ministers on 1 Dec 2026. The European Parliament plans to adopt its position on 27 Apr 2027. The act is unlikely to bite before about 2029.

sps.track: Government steps to move new data centres outside Tokyo and Osaka, the share built there, and whether grid connection times in the regions stay well below Tokyo's.
sps.trigger: Positive if a meaningful share of new capacity is committed outside Tokyo and Osaka, and regional connection times stay well below Tokyo's.
sps.headline: About 90% in Tokyo and Osaka
sps.summary: About 90% of Japan's data centres are in the Tokyo and Osaka areas. Nine regions are reported certified as cluster locations in September 2026. Connections take 3 to 5 years in Osaka where spare capacity exists, against 8 to 10 in Tokyo
sps.latest: About 90% of Japan's data centres by floor area are in the Tokyo and Osaka areas, according to a press report of June 2025. On 24 Apr 2026 the economy ministry shortlisted nine regions for data centre clusters: Hokkaido, Akita, Miyagi, Tochigi, Ibaraki, Toyama, Kagawa, Fukuoka and Kagoshima. Press reports say all nine were certified in the first batch in September 2026, with a second batch planned by March 2027; one of the cities concerned confirms its own certification. The share is updated rarely, so this signpost follows policy steps and announced projects. On connection times: Tokyo takes 8 to 10 years to connect a large data centre. In Osaka, 3 to 5 years applies only where the grid already has spare capacity. Osaka Prefecture's paper of 9 Oct 2026 says the Osaka Bay coast has almost no spare capacity, that strengthening the grid there takes about 8 years, and that large headroom will not appear even afterwards. It gives more than 10 years for Keihanna, and for southern Osaka beyond the few hundred megawatts it can take now. Saito could gain gigawatt-scale capacity if grid work is tied to site development. The paper predates the 12 Nov 2026 baseline.
sps.next: Second batch of certified regions by March 2027; the grid operator's next capacity map

sps.headline: About 60% around Seoul

sps.latest: Savills Korea counted 165 data centres in Korea in 2024, 60.4% of them in the Seoul capital region, and reports commercial sites spreading to other regions. In August 2026 the energy ministry and Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) presented 11 regional electricity price zones that favour areas outside the capital. About half of permitted data centre projects in the capital region are reported stalled by community opposition. On the exemption threshold: A draft decree published for comment on 20 Nov 2026 sets the exemption at 50 megawatts of contracted power or less for AI data centres built, expanded or converted outside the capital region, the bottom of the 50 to 100 megawatt range that was under discussion. The government also plans to let data centres in designated special zones skip the non-technical review regardless of size, through a change to the assessment rules. Comments are open until 30 Dec 2026.

calls.bottom_line: Water rises from Moderate to Severe after 2030: growth is concentrated in water-stressed hubs, and in droughts governments put households first. Thailand's reuse rule and Johor's reclaimed water are the main offsets; India's hub states have no binding water rules.

insight: To 2030, power is the binding constraint in North America, Europe and North Asia. After 2030 it eases in North America and North Asia, but Europe's core hubs wait for grid fixes into the 2030s, and growth moving into water-stressed areas makes water the rising constraint in southern Europe and South and Southeast Asia.
coverage_note: The tracker follows eight region and constraint pairs: the four where the rating changes between 2026–30 and beyond 2030, the two where a Severe rating persists, and the two Moderate pairs that complete the picture for North America and Europe, where the question is whether Moderate eases to Minor or intensifies to Severe.
